title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is working on quadratic residues modulo primes, i.e. for which primes P a given number a is a square mod P. In §22 he set T = (2q+1)^2 − 4at and claimed that a is a quadratic residue of every prime of the form 4as + T or 4as − T.

§23 (Cor. 1): The admissible T are just the odd squares reduced mod 4a. So one needs only the finitely many values below 4a; all others arise by adding multiples of 4a.

§24 (Cor. 2): Since a is a residue of such a prime P = 2m+1, some x^2 − a y^2 is divisible by P. Hence (Euler's criterion) P divides a^m − 1.

§25 (Scholion): The number of classes T depends on whether a is prime or composite. The prime case must be settled first.

§26 (Theorem): If a = 2α+1 is prime, there are exactly α values of T below 4a. Correspondingly α of the residue classes ≡ 1 (mod 4) prime to a are excluded; these are called Θ in §27.

Proof:
- The T come from the odd squares 1, 9, …, (2α−1)^2.
- Larger odd squares give nothing new: (a+β)^2 − (a−β)^2 = 4aβ.
- These α squares are distinct mod 4a. Indeed (2i+1)^2 − (2j+1)^2 = 4(i−j)(i+j+1) and i+j+1 < a.
- Among 1 … 4a there are 2α+1 numbers ≡ 1 (mod 4). One of them is divisible by a, leaving 2α.
- So exactly half are T and half are excluded Θ.

In modern terms: the classes of primes P (P ≡ 1 or 3 mod 4, read as ±T) for which (a/P) = 1 form a union of residue classes mod 4a. These are the classes ±(odd squares) mod 4a. Their number is φ(4a)/4 per sign, i.e. half of the classes ≡ 1 mod 4 prime to a. This is Euler's 'mod 4a' formulation of quadratic reciprocity. The next page tabulates T and Θ for a = 2, 3, 5, …, 29.
errors: The 'Demonstratio' of §22, on which §§23-26 rest, is conditional. Write the prime as P = 4a(s∓t) ± (2q+1)^2; then 4a(s±t) ≡ ±(2q+1)^2 (mod P). This only shows that a·(s±t) is a residue (taking −1 into account). To conclude that a itself is a residue one needs the §21 'Conclusio' that all prime factors of residues of the form p are themselves residues. That was supported only by examples (§20), and is essentially equivalent to quadratic reciprocity. So the theorem is unproved, as is well known for Euler's reciprocity statements.

§26 proof: reduction of arbitrary odd squares to those below a^2 is shown only via the reflection (a+β)^2 ≡ (a−β)^2. The periodicity k → k+2a (difference 4a(k+a)) is used tacitly. This is a minor gap.
Implicit conditions are not stated: the prime must not divide a, and for the −T case one needs P ≡ 3 (mod 4).

ideas.what: Primes having a as a quadratic residue are exactly those ≡ ±(odd square) mod 4a
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity (Euler's form: (a/p) depends only on p mod 4a)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjectured 1744-1751, stated in Opuscula Analytica 1783), proved by Gauss 1796/1801; Legendre's symmetric form
ideas.where_published: E164 / E552 'Observationes circa divisionem quadratorum per numeros primos' and this paper E557 (Opusc. Anal. I, 1783)

ideas.what: a a residue mod 2m+1 implies a^m ≡ 1 mod 2m+1
ideas.where_published: E262 and related papers on residues

ideas.what: For a an odd prime, exactly half of the classes ≡1 mod 4 (prime to a) mod 4a are odd squares
ideas.modern_name: Counting quadratic residue classes / index-2 subgroup

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known mod-4a formulation of quadratic reciprocity with a routine class count. It is documented in histories (Weil, Lemmermeyer, Edwards), and nothing on the page appears absent from the literature.
